content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is the leading cause of maternal mortality globally. Prophylactic administration of uterotonic agents is a standard practice to prevent PPH, with the World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommending 10 IU of oxytocin administered either intramuscularly or intravenously. Despite the availability of several uterotonic agents, there remains uncertainty regarding which agent is the most effective while minimizing side effects. This study is an updated Cochrane Review, incorporating data from a recent large WHO trial, to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of various uterotonic agents. The primary objective of this analysis was to determine the most effective uterotonic agent(s) for preventing PPH with the least side effects and to rank these agents based on their efficacy and safety profiles. The study included randomized controlled trials and cluster-randomized trials comparing uterotonic agents, placebo, or no treatment. Quasi-randomized trials were excluded. Data were collected and analyzed independently by at least three reviewers, and both pairwise and network meta-analyses were performed to assess the relative effects and rankings of the agents. The network meta-analysis included 196 trials involving 135,559 women across 53 countries, with most trials conducted in hospital settings and involving vaginal births. The analysis demonstrated that all uterotonic agents were effective in preventing PPH ≥ 500 mL compared to placebo or no treatment. The three highest-ranked agents for preventing PPH ≥ 500 mL were the combination of ergometrine plus oxytocin, the combination of misoprostol plus oxytocin, and carbetocin. Moderate-certainty evidence indicated that ergometrine plus oxytocin (RR 0.70) and carbetocin (RR 0.72) reduced the risk of PPH ≥ 500 mL compared to oxytocin. Low-certainty evidence suggested that misoprostol plus oxytocin (RR 0.70) also reduced this risk. However, misoprostol, injectable prostaglandins, and ergometrine alone showed little or no difference compared to oxytocin for this outcome. For PPH ≥ 1000 mL, all agents except ergometrine and injectable prostaglandins were effective compared to placebo or no treatment. High-certainty evidence suggested that ergometrine plus oxytocin (RR 0.83) and misoprostol plus oxytocin (RR 0.88) made little or no difference compared to oxytocin. Misoprostol alone was less effective than oxytocin for preventing PPH ≥ 1000 mL (RR 1.19, high certainty). Despite these findings, the combination of ergometrine plus oxytocin, misoprostol plus oxytocin, and carbetocin were the highest-ranked agents for preventing PPH ≥ 1000 mL. The combination of misoprostol plus oxytocin reduced the need for additional uterotonics (RR 0.56, high certainty) and likely reduced the risk of blood transfusion (RR 0.51, moderate certainty) compared to oxytocin. Carbetocin, injectable prostaglandins, and ergometrine plus oxytocin may also reduce the need for additional uterotonics, but the certainty of evidence was low. No significant differences were observed between agents for maternal deaths or severe morbidity, as these outcomes were rare in the included trials. However, the two combination regimens were associated with notable side effects. Misoprostol plus oxytocin increased the risk of vomiting (RR 2.11, high certainty) and fever (RR 3.14, moderate certainty) compared to oxytocin. Ergometrine plus oxytocin also increased the risk of vomiting (RR 2.93, moderate certainty) and had variable effects on hypertension, with low-certainty evidence for this outcome. Subgroup analyses did not reveal significant differences based on mode of birth, healthcare setting, PPH risk, misoprostol dose, or oxytocin regimen. In conclusion, all uterotonic agents were generally effective in preventing PPH compared to placebo or no treatment. The combination of ergometrine plus oxytocin, carbetocin, and misoprostol plus oxytocin demonstrated additional benefits compared to oxytocin alone. However, the combination regimens were associated with significant side effects. Carbetocin may offer advantages over oxytocin for certain outcomes without increasing side effects.
